Legislation Applicable to Pacific Salmon and Ecosystems (LAPSE)

Technical Manual and Methodology

Joe Enns, Cory Lagasse, Daniel Gillis, Marina Wright

2026-03-17

Interactive App

⚠️ Disclaimer: None of the information presented in this document qualifies as legal advice. The authors are aquatic biologists with limited legal training. This tool is intended for research and informational purposes only.

1 Overview

Pacific salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.) populations are generally declining in Canada, while the number of populations monitored continues to drop, despite considerable attention toward policies and recovery programs for salmon conservation. The causes of these declines are varied — including loss or degradation of freshwater habitat, climate change, hatchery pressures, and harvest — and addressing them requires coordinated action across a fragmented governance landscape where federal jurisdiction over fisheries intersects with provincial authority over freshwater habitat.

The Legislation Applicable to Pacific Salmon and Ecosystems (LAPSE) framework was developed to bridge this complexity. It is a systematic process and open-source tool that maps Canadian federal and British Columbian provincial legislation to standardized anthropogenic threat categories, enabling stewardship practitioners to navigate the regulatory landscape governing Pacific salmon and their ecosystems. This document serves as the technical manual and methodology reference for the LAPSE process, database, and associated tools.

For results, discussion, and case studies, refer to the primary publication:

Enns, J., Lagasse, C., Gillis, D., and Wright, M. (2026). An interface between statutes and salmon: the Legislation Applicable to Pacific Salmon and Ecosystems (LAPSE) framework. [Journal pending]

🔗 LAPSE Pipeline (R scripts) including all source code, data processing scripts, keyword lists, and the SQLite database, is available at: https://github.com/dfo-pacific-science/LAPSE_pipeline

🔗 LAPSE Dashboard (interactive tool) is available at: https://dfo-pacific-science.github.io/LAPSE_dashboard/

🔗 LAPSE About page: https://dfo-pacific-science.github.io/LAPSE_dashboard/LAPSE-Dashboard-About.html

2 Purpose and Scope

2.1 Objectives

This framework and tool were developed to decode the complexity between threats to Pacific salmon and corresponding environmental legislation by creating an interface between regulatory language and anthropogenic threat categories. The specific objectives were to:

  1. create a process and tool to categorize specific legislation by anthropogenic threats to Pacific salmon;
  2. assess legislative factors by threat categorization across federal and provincial jurisdictions; and
  3. provide a framework to support systematic and critical reviews of the strengths and shortcomings of regulations with respect to salmon threats.

2.2 What LAPSE covers

LAPSE accumulates and categorizes Canadian federal and British Columbian provincial legislation relevant to Pacific salmon and habitat stewardship. For this study, the term legislation (or statutes) refers collectively to acts, regulations, codes, and orders. The scope is limited to legislation as written; this study does not verify the implementation or enforcement of accumulated statutes in practice.

Legislation is used as the primary unit of analysis — rather than policy — because legislation is a better indicator of a jurisdiction’s long-term commitment to natural resource stewardship (Bogetti and Mason 2025). Policies are formal statements about how the government of the day plans to execute legislative requirements and are more prone to changes in the political, administrative, and budgetary landscape, while legislation is subject to due process or a parliamentary vote. Specific departmental policy frameworks and processes were not assessed.

2.3 What LAPSE does not cover

The following were outside the scope of this legislative review in terms of feasibility and timelines, though some may overlap with included federal or provincial legislation:

  • Indigenous legislation and land claims agreements (with the exception of select Final Agreement Acts enacted as federal or provincial statutes)
  • Yukon Territorial legislation
  • Municipal bylaws
  • International conventions and treaties

3 LAPSE Process Overview

The LAPSE framework follows a linear pipeline from legislation collection through to the interactive dashboard. The eight major steps below describe the complete process; subsequent sections of this document provide full technical detail for each step.

Figure: The LAPSE process pipeline from legislation collection to end use. Teal headers indicate the six major phases; detail nodes describe the inputs, steps, and outputs within each phase.

3.1 The six phases

Phase 1 — Collect. Relevant Canadian federal and British Columbian provincial legislation is identified through a step-wise keyword search on CanLII, beginning with Pacific salmon-specific terms and expanding outward via word frequency analysis and IUCN threat terminology. HTML files for all relevant statutes are downloaded directly from the federal and BC provincial legislation portals. The result is 196 statutes (87 federal, 109 provincial) stored in data/legislation_html/.

Phase 2 — Build database. Two R scripts convert the raw HTML files into structured SQLite tables. 01_database_legislation.R extracts metadata (jurisdiction, legislation type, act name) from each file’s HTML structure. 02_database_paragraphs.R parses each statute clause-by-clause, extracting paragraph text, section numbers, and headings while filtering out footnotes, amendment references, and editorial sections. Outputs are the LegislationMetadata and LegislationParagraphs tables in output/legislation.db.

Phase 3 — Develop keywords. Five keyword CSV files are developed and refined through an iterative process drawing on IUCN–CMP threat definitions, word frequency analyses of collected legislation, and researcher expert judgment. Keywords are reviewed and revised continuously — single-word ambiguities are replaced with more specific bigrams or trigrams, domain-irrelevant terms are removed, and salmon-relevant terms absent from IUCN definitions (e.g., riparian) are added manually.

Phase 4 — Label. 03_database_labels.R tokenizes all paragraph and heading text using quanteda, compounds multi-word keyword phrases (longest-first), then matches four keyword lists independently against each clause. IUCN labels are automatically duplicated as their corresponding Management Domain labels via a lookup table. Scope values (1–4) are assigned to each label row. After deduplication, all results are written to the paragraph_label_table.

Phase 5 — Filter actionable clauses. 05_actionable_clauses.R applies a seven-step filtering pipeline to the full labelled dataset to identify the subset of act clauses that authorize or instruct an official to create a specific regulatory product (plan, licence, designation, etc.). The filter requires a responsible official keyword to appear before a mandatory or discretionary verb within five words. Results are written to the actionable_clauses table and exported as output/actionable_clauses.csv.

Phase 6 — Explore. The complete legislation.db database is served through the LAPSE Dashboard, which allows users to filter legislation by management domain, jurisdiction, keyword search, clause type, responsible official, and discretion type — viewing highlighted legislative text and dynamic visualizations. Filtered results can be downloaded as XLSX. The database also underlies the primary publication analyses and can support recovery planning, Recovery Potential Assessments, and threat-specific regulatory reviews.

4 Data Sources

4.1 Canadian Legal Information Institute (CanLII)

The primary resource for locating and reviewing Canadian legislation was the Canadian Legal Information Institute (CanLII):

https://www.canlii.org/

CanLII provides a comprehensive, searchable database of federal and provincial legislation. It was used as the entry point for the step-wise keyword search process used to identify relevant statutes (see Section 6). Users can search by keyword within any jurisdiction and view individual keyword occurrences in context within any statute.

4.2 Federal legislation portal

Official HTML files for Canadian federal legislation were downloaded directly from the Department of Justice Canada:

https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/

Responsible ministers for each federal act were confirmed using the Table of Public Statutes and Responsible Ministers:

https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/PDF/tops/eng/TOPS.pdf

4.3 British Columbia provincial legislation portal

Official HTML files for British Columbian provincial legislation were downloaded from the BC Laws database:

https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/content/complete/statreg/

Responsible ministers for each provincial act were confirmed using the Acts – Ministers’ Responsibilities resource:

https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/content/amr/amr/

5.2 The jurisdictional context

The patchwork of legislative authority is most prominent in Pacific salmon management due to the species’ geographically widespread, anadromous life cycles that span international boundaries and freshwater and marine ecosystems. While salmon populations and fisheries are regulated federally, water use, watercourse alterations, and the corresponding aquatic habitat are managed provincially. The federal government also regulates navigable waters within provincial boundaries (Becklumb 2013; Swerdfager and Olive 2023), and both levels of government have authority to designate protected areas.

British Columbia is more decentralized than other provinces — particularly with respect to species at risk — because relevant provisions are spread over the greatest number of statutes and regulations (Bogetti and Mason 2025). This means that a single human activity (e.g., forestry) can engage multiple acts across multiple ministries, making the full legislative picture difficult to navigate without a framework like LAPSE.

6 Management Domain Framework

6.1 IUCN–CMP threat classification background

The IUCN and the Conservation Measures Partnership (CMP) developed the IUCN–CMP Direct Threats Classification Version 4.0 (Salafsky et al. 2024), which defines threats as “current or future human activities or altered natural phenomena that affect one or more ecosystems or species of interest.” The classification uses a three-level hierarchical structure analogous to a Linnean taxonomy:

  • Level 1 — Broadest categories (e.g., 2. Agriculture & Aquaculture)
  • Level 2 — Subcategories (e.g., 2.4 Marine & Freshwater Aquaculture)
  • Level 3 — Most specific sub-subcategories (not used in this assessment)

This classification is widely applied in IUCN Red List assessments, COSEWIC status assessments, and DFO Recovery Potential Assessments (RPAs) for Pacific salmon populations.

6.2 Why management domains were needed

Canadian and British Columbian legislation has been enacted on a sector-by-sector basis and does not align neatly with IUCN–CMP Level 1 categories. The Level 2 categories fit better with legislative categories but still required lumping and splitting to match how legislation is organized in practice. Additionally, not all aspects of salmon management connect to a direct human threat: topics such as restoration, species status, spatial designation, and governance administration may encompass all threats or none. To capture both threat and non-threat categories, a schema of management domains was created, defined as “discrete areas of administrative concern.”

6.3 Management domains and IUCN–CMP alignment

Management domains and corresponding IUCN–CMP Level 2 threat categories. Restoration, Spatial Designation, and Species Status and Assessment do not correspond to direct threat categories but represent important governance areas for Pacific salmon stewardship.

7 Legislation Collection Process

7.1 Overview of the collection workflow

Relevant legislation was compiled through a step-wise keyword search process using CanLII, designed to be publicly accessible, automated, and repeatable as legislation changes over time. The collection steps were:

  1. Query Pacific salmon-specific terms in CanLII (e.g., salmon, Chinook, sockeye, coho, steelhead)
  2. Extract additional adjacent keywords from salmon-specific legislation using word frequency analysis (see Section 6.2)
  3. Query extracted keywords and IUCN threat description wording in CanLII to find adjacent legislation
  4. Filter results regionally (excluding provinces other than British Columbia)
  5. Download HTML files for relevant legislation directly from government portals

7.2 Word frequency extraction for adjacent keywords

Popular practitioner language may not appear in legal text due to the age and generality of legislation. To capture salmon-relevant terms that actually occur in statutes, a word frequency analysis was performed on salmon-specific legislation using the udpipe R package (Wijffels 2025), extracting unigrams, bigrams, and trigrams that co-occur with salmon-specific terms. These extracted keywords were combined with wording from the IUCN–CMP Direct Threats Classification 4.0 and queried in CanLII to identify additional relevant legislation.

7.3 Verification via CanLII

Through the CanLII website, individual keywords can be queried within any chosen statute, allowing users to quickly assess the context of a keyword in the legislation and determine whether a section is relevant to Pacific salmon stewardship. This verification step was applied during collection to screen out statutes where keyword matches occurred in contexts unrelated to salmon.

7.4 Legislation type and ministry assignment

Script: 01_database_legislation.R

Jurisdiction was determined automatically from HTML metadata in each downloaded file: federal legislation was identified by the meta[name='description'] tag containing "Federal laws of Canada", while provincial legislation was identified by the meta[name='breadcrumb'] tag containing "British Columbia". Legislation type (Act, Regulation, Order, Code) was inferred from the legislation name using pattern matching on terms “Regulation/Regulations”, “Order”, “Act”, and “Code”. For non-Act statutes, the parent act name was extracted from the HTML enabling-act element (p.EnablingAct a or div#actname h2). Responsible ministers were assigned using:

  • Federal: Table of Public Statutes and Responsible Ministers (Department of Justice Canada 2026)
  • Provincial: Acts – Ministers’ Responsibilities (Province of British Columbia 2025)

8 Parsing and Database Structure

8.1 Legistics and the clause as the unit of analysis

The individual clause was used as the sample unit for assignment into management domains and other attributes. Typological device structure and definitions were derived from the Government of Canada’s Legistics Paragraphing guide:

https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/rp-pr/csj-sjc/legis-redact/legistics/p3p1.html

“Clause” in this study refers to individual HTML paragraph elements (<p>), which may correspond to subclauses, sections, subsections, or opening words (chapeau or umbrella text). The hierarchy of elements from largest to smallest is: heading → section → subsection → clause → subclause.

8.2 HTML parsing with rvest

Script: 02_database_paragraphs.R

Legislation on Canadian and British Columbian government websites is structured such that each clause appears as a separate HTML paragraph element. HTML files were parsed using R and the rvest package (Wickham 2025), targeting the following node selector to capture the full range of paragraph contexts across legislation formats:

html_nodes("p, div p, dl p, dd p, li p, ul p, dfn p, a p, span p")

Section headings were extracted from marginal notes and heading elements:

html_nodes("p.MarginalNote, h4, h3, h2")

Each paragraph was assigned the text of its nearest preceding heading using XPath lookup. The editorial prefix "Marginal note:" is stripped from heading text before storage.

8.2.1 Section number extraction

Section numbers were extracted from each paragraph node using a four-strategy cascade, applied in order until a valid section number was found:

Section number extraction strategies applied in cascade to each parsed paragraph (02_database_paragraphs.R).

Strategy

Description

1 — Inline text (primary)

Extracts a number matching the regex ^(\d+(?:\.\d+){0,3}) from the very start of the paragraph text. Handles complex section numbering formats including 1.01, 1.01.01, and 3.12.2.

2 — Structured HTML elements

Extracts section numbers from structured HTML span elements: span.secnum span.secnumholder b, a.sectionLabel span.sectionLabel, span.secnum b, and span.secnumholder.

3 — Section keyword prefix

Extracts numbers following the literal text 'Section' at the paragraph start using a lookbehind regex.

4 — Bracketed reference

Extracts numbers from bracketed references of the form [(X.XX)] at the paragraph start.

Schedule and Appendix headers (e.g., Schedule A, Appendix B) are detected and used to prefix section numbers within that block (e.g., section 3 within Schedule A becomes A-3). The header itself is not stored as a paragraph.

8.2.2 Content filtering

Several categories of paragraph content were excluded before writing to the database:

Content filtering rules applied during HTML parsing (02_database_paragraphs.R).

Filter

Description

Footer / metadata

Paragraphs matching patterns such as "King's Printer", "Queen's Printer", "Copyright ©", "Victoria, British Columbia, Canada", and numeric-only text under 5 characters.

Amendment references

Paragraphs fully enclosed in square brackets (e.g., [am. B.C. Reg. ...], [en. ...], [Repealed ...]) or matching statute citation patterns such as S.C. 2001, c. 26 and S.B.C. formats.

Editorial headings

Paragraphs under headings indicating non-legislative editorial content are excluded. Affected headings include: RELATED PROVISIONS, AMENDMENTS NOT IN FORCE, TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS, COMING INTO FORCE, CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENTS, COORDINATING AMENDMENTS, TABLE OF CONTENTS, and CONDITIONAL AMENDMENTS.

Repeal / revocation language

Paragraphs containing the words repeal, repealed, revoked, Marginal note, or Not in force are removed in a post-processing filter pass.

No section number

Paragraphs to which no section number could be assigned by any of the four extraction strategies are excluded.

9 Keyword and Keyphrase Development

9.1 Sources of keywords

The management domain and IUCN–CMP threat matching process pivoted around established lists of keywords and phrases. Keywords must be specific enough to match an IUCN–CMP threat, yet general enough to appear across multiple acts and regulations spanning many decades of legal language. Keywords were derived from three sources:

  1. IUCN–CMP Direct Threats Classification 4.0 examples and definitions (Salafsky et al. 2024)
  2. Word frequency analyses (unigrams, bigrams, and trigrams) of all collected legislation, performed using the udpipe R package (Wijffels 2025)
  3. Iterative researcher input and revision based on domain expertise in Pacific salmon stewardship

The full keyword and keyphrase lists by management domain and clause type are available in Appendix II and Appendix III of the primary publication and in the data/ directory of the project repository.

9.2 Iterative revision process

Keyword development required iterative researcher revision because of the varied context of natural language. Words used in IUCN–CMP threat definitions may be irrelevant to salmon stewardship in the legislative context, and single words in particular can have multiple meanings leading to over-assignment of categories. Two illustrative examples from the primary publication:

  • Removed keyword — “landfill”: Listed in IUCN–CMP examples for 1.2 Commercial & Industrial Areas in the context of the physical footprint of landfill sites. In collected legislation, “landfill” appears primarily in effluent and water pollution contexts, which are better classified under Pollution. Including it added many clauses outside the tool’s scope, so it was removed.

  • Added keyword — “riparian”: Highly relevant to salmon habitat stewardship in British Columbia, yet absent from IUCN–CMP threat examples and word frequency analyses of other legislation. Added solely from researchers’ expert judgment.

9.3 Managing ambiguous keywords

Single-word keywords can cause mis-categorization in unexpected ways. For example, “stock” is important for the Fisheries management domain (referring to salmon populations) but also appears in the context of business holdings, freight cars, and livestock. To address this, outputs were reviewed iteratively and keyword revision was a continuous process to:

  • find more accurate bigram or trigram alternatives that reduce false positives (e.g., “fish stock”, “salmon stock”)
  • remove keywords where clauses are already matched via more specific alternatives
  • capture relevant word variations (plural, past tense, possessive)

10.2 Tokenization and keyword matching

Script: 03_database_labels.R

Keyword matching is performed using the quanteda package (Benoit et al. 2018) rather than simple text search. This allows multi-word phrases (bigrams, trigrams) to be matched as compound tokens before single-word matching is applied, preventing shorter keywords from consuming parts of longer, more specific phrases.

All keyword CSV files are pre-sorted by decreasing keyword length before compounding, so that the most specific phrases are matched first. The matching process is applied independently to both paragraph text and heading text for each clause, then the resulting label rows are combined and deduplicated. This ensures that management domain labels are captured even when the relevant terminology appears only in the section heading and not in the clause body.

The processing workflow for each text source is:

# 1. Normalize text: lowercase, collapse whitespace, remove punctuation
cleaned_text <- str_squish(tolower(str_replace_all(text, "[[:punct:]]", " ")))

# 2. Build quanteda corpus and tokenize
tokens_obj <- tokens(corpus(data.frame(text = cleaned_text)), remove_punct = TRUE)

# 3. Compound multi-word phrases (longest-first order)
tokens_obj <- tokens_compound(tokens_obj, pattern = phrase(iucn_l2_keywords$keyword))
tokens_obj <- tokens_compound(tokens_obj, pattern = phrase(governance_keywords$keyword))
tokens_obj <- tokens_compound(tokens_obj, pattern = phrase(salmon_scope_keywords$keyword))
tokens_obj <- tokens_compound(tokens_obj, pattern = phrase(clause_type_keywords$keyword))

# 4. Match each keyword list against token sets (vectorized, batches of 1000 paragraphs)
# 5. Assign label_type and label_value from value_column in each keyword CSV
# 6. Combine paragraph and heading label tables; deduplicate by (paragraph_id, label_type, keyword, label_value)

10.2.1 IUCN-to-Management Domain duplication

After IUCN labels are assigned, each IUCN label is also used to generate a corresponding Management Domain label via the management_domain_threat_table lookup. For example, a clause matched to IUCN threat 9.1 Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution automatically also receives a Pollution Management Domain label. This dual-labelling enables users to search by either the standardized IUCN threat or the more practitioner-oriented management domain, and enables co-occurrence analysis across management domains (see primary publication, Figure 8).

10.3 Salmon-specific scope

A scope classification categorizes each matched clause by its directness of application to Pacific salmon, determined by the matched keyword. Scope is stored per label row in the paragraph_label_table.

Salmon-specific scope categories, keyword sources, and definitions.

Scope

Keyword Source

Definition

1 – Salmon

salmon_scope_keywords.csv

Refers to Pacific salmon specifically (e.g., salmon, Chinook, sockeye, coho, steelhead). Assigned based solely on salmon scope keywords, independently of management domain.

2 – Fish

iucn_l2_keywords.csv / management_domain_threat_table.csv

Refers to fish that include salmon (e.g., fish, anadromous, fish habitat). Aligns to IUCN threats via scope value in management_domain_threat_table, unless clause is already Scope 1.

3 – Habitat

iucn_l2_keywords.csv / management_domain_threat_table.csv

Refers to any habitat that includes salmon habitat (e.g., watercourse, riparian, watershed). Aligns to IUCN threats via scope value in management_domain_threat_table, unless already Scope 1 or 2.

4 – Governance

governance_keywords.csv

Refers to administrative processes and governance structure. Applied in a separate matching pass using governance_keywords.csv.

10.4 Clause type classification

The legal character and intent of each clause is classified by clause type, enabling users to filter to, for example, all prohibition clauses within a given management domain. Clause type keywords are provided in data/clause_type_keywords.csv.

Prohibition, Restriction, or Limitation

Prohibits or limits a specific action or activity

Like management domains, clause types can co-occur within a single clause — a clause may simultaneously receive Authorization and Instruction labels if keywords for both are present.

10.5 Actionable clause filtering

Script: 05_actionable_clauses.R

A subset of clauses was further filtered to identify actionable clauses — defined as clauses that authorize or instruct an official to create or establish a regulatory product (e.g., a water licence, land designation, or management plan). This subset is useful for identifying specific legislative tools that could be invoked to address a given salmon threat. The pipeline applies the following steps in sequence:

Actionable clause filtering pipeline steps applied in sequence by 05_actionable_clauses.R.

Step

Description

1. Acts only

Only Acts are included (legislation_type == 'Act'). Regulations and orders are implementations of act clauses and are excluded from this subset.

2. Management Domain label required

Paragraphs must have at least one Management Domain label in paragraph_label_table.

3. Clause Type filter

Only paragraphs with at least one of these Clause Type labels are retained: Designation; Instruction; Licence, Permitting, & Exemptions; Authorization & Mandate.

4. Intersection

The three filters above (Acts, Management Domain, Clause Type) are intersected, keeping only paragraphs passing all three.

5. Exclude definition headings

Paragraphs where the Heading field contains the word 'definition' (case-insensitive) are removed to avoid interpretive or definitional clauses.

6. Responsible official keywords

A curated list of responsible-official terms from actionable_clause_keywords (category: responsible official) is matched via whole-word regex. Paragraphs must contain at least one match (e.g., minister, director, officer, board).

7. Discretionary language keywords

A list of discretionary and mandatory verbs from actionable_clause_keywords (category: discretionary language) is matched via whole-word regex. Paragraphs must contain at least one match (e.g., may, must, shall, authorize).

6b. Word-order constraint

To confirm the official is the grammatical subject of the verb: (a) the official keyword must appear before the discretionary verb, and (b) the verb must occur within 5 words of the end of the official keyword. Evaluated via character-position and word-count functions applied to each paragraph.

8. Extract actionable attributes

Three attributes are extracted per qualifying paragraph via regex pattern matching: actionable_type (regulatory instrument type: regulation, plan, permit, licence, designation, reserve, park, protected area, agreement, report, assessment, etc., returned semicolon-delimited); responsible_official (all matched official keywords, semicolon-delimited); discretion_type (each discretionary keyword mapped to 'mandatory' or 'discretionary', semicolon-delimited).

9–10. Merge metadata and export

Results are joined with LegislationMetadata to add act_name and jurisdiction, then exported to both output/actionable_clauses.csv and the actionable_clauses table in the SQLite database.

11 Reproducibility and Versioning

11.1 Repeatability by design

The LAPSE process was designed to be publicly accessible, automated, and repeatable as legislation changes over time. The collection and parsing pipeline can be re-run to update the database when new legislation is enacted, existing legislation is amended, IUCN–CMP threat categories are updated, or keyword lists are revised. All scripts, keyword CSV files, and the SQLite database are version-controlled in the project GitHub repository:

https://github.com/dfo-pacific-science/salmon_management_domains_compendium

11.3 Transparency of researcher subjectivity

Researcher subjectivity influences the process at two primary points: (1) decisions about whether a given statute is relevant to Pacific salmon stewardship (legislation inclusion), and (2) decisions about which keywords to include, remove, or modify (keyword list development). Using explicit, documented keyword lists allows this subjectivity to be acknowledged, reported, and reproduced. The keyword CSV files are available in the data/ directory of the repository, enabling other researchers to review decisions, propose revisions, and re-run the process with alternative keyword configurations.

12 Known Limitations

1. Keyword-based matching is not semantic. Keyword matching identifies the presence of a term but does not parse legal intent or the surrounding sentence structure. A keyword may appear in an unrelated context (e.g., “stock” in a livestock regulation). Iterative review and bigram/trigram refinement mitigate but do not eliminate this issue.

2. Clause scope does not reflect regulatory effectiveness. The count of statutes, sections, or clauses matched to a management domain is not a measure of the quality or effectiveness of legislation (Ray et al. 2021). A management domain with many matched clauses may still have weak or discretionary regulatory coverage.

3. Implementation and enforcement are not assessed. This study reports legislation as written. It does not verify whether responsible agencies actively implement or enforce provisions, nor does it assess the adequacy of resources or capacity available to do so.

4. Policy is excluded. Departmental policy frameworks (e.g., DFO’s Wild Salmon Policy) are not included, despite significantly shaping how legislation is applied in practice.

5. Scope of jurisdictions. Indigenous legislation, Yukon legislation, municipal bylaws, and international conventions are not included, despite their importance to Pacific salmon stewardship.

6. Legislation currency. HTML files were downloaded from government portals at a specific point in time. Legislation is periodically amended and consolidated; users should verify that referenced legislation reflects the current consolidated version.

7. IUCN–CMP version alignment. RPAs and COSEWIC assessments used in the primary publication were conducted under earlier versions of the IUCN–CMP classification. Threat categories were updated to align with version 4.0 where possible, but minor inconsistencies may remain.
